subject: beta regression on data with measurement error

messages.author: 773b8742e60f5bfa
messages.subject: beta regression on data with measurement error
parts:
Hi, 

I'm trying beta regression on some data with measurement error. I ran Stan with the model below. No error message was produced in the compiling, but it did not run at all in the sampling.
Any comments will be greatly appreciated.
Thanks.

data {
  int<lower=1> Ndata ;
  vector[Ndata] xobs ; // observed x
  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[Ndata] y ; //response 
}
parameters {
  real a; // parameter of linear predictor
  real b; // a+bx
  real<lower=0> ph; // sigma
}
model {
    vector<lower=0,upper=1>[Ndata] mu;
    vector<lower=0>[Ndata] beta_a;
    vector<lower=0>[Ndata] beta_b;
    vector[Ndata] xtrue;
    a ~ normal(0, 1.0e+2);
    b ~ normal(0, 1.0e+2);
    ph ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);
    for (n in 1:Ndata) {
      xobs[n] ~ normal(xtrue[n],0.01);
      mu[n] <- inv_logit(a + b*xtrue[n]);
    }  
  beta_a <- mu * ph;
  beta_b <- (1-mu) * ph;
  y ~ beta(beta_a, beta_b);
}

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: beta regression on data with measurement error
parts:
It would help to see the error message, but at a minimum, you need to declare xtrue in the parameters block. So, I think it would sample if you did
 
data {
 int<lower=1> Ndata ;
vector[Ndata] xobs ; // observed x
real<lower=0> error_sd; // possibly 0.01

vector<lower=0, upper=1>[Ndata] y ; //response
}
parameters {
 real a; // parameter of linear predictor
 real b; // a+bx
real<lower=0> ph; // sigma

vector[Ndata] xtrue;
}
model {
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[Ndata] mu;
  // these priors are too diffuse and gamma(0,0) has a weird shape

a ~ normal(0, 1.0e+2);
  b ~ normal(0, 1.0e+2);

ph ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  xobs ~ normal(xtrue, error_sd);
for (n in 1:Ndata) {

mu[n] <- inv_logit(a + b*xtrue[n]);
  }

y ~ beta(mu * ph, (1-mu) * ph);
}

but it might not sample well because of those priors. As Andrew would say, use Cauchy priors for everything.

Ben

messages.author: 773b8742e60f5bfa
messages.subject: Re: beta regression on data with measurement error
parts:
Thank you so much for your help, Ben.

I modified the code with your suggestion, and it ran without any trouble. One step further I'd like to add measurement error as modelled as below. I managed to run the code, but it performs very poorly. I wonder if you have any suggestion to improve the peformance.
  
# data generation
set.seed(999)
n <- 50
gain <- 1.0
threshold <- 0.0
sx <- 0.5  # measurement error

xtrue <- runif(n, -3, 3) # true value
xerr <- xtrue + rnorm(n, 0, sx) # measurement error

logit_y <- 1/(1+exp(-gain*(xtrue-threshold)))
ph <- 1.0
beta_a <- logit_y*ph
beta_b <- (1-logit_y)*ph
y <- rbeta(n, beta_a, beta_b) 
y[y==1.0] = 1.0-1.0e-4

model_string = "
data {
  int<lower=1> Ndata ;
  vector[Ndata] x ;

vector<lower=0, upper=1>[Ndata] y ;
}

parameters {
  real a; // parameter of linear predictor
  real b; // a+bx
  real<lower=0> ph; // sigma
real<lower=0> sx; // sigma of x

vector[Ndata] xtrue;
}
model {
    vector<lower=0,upper=1>[Ndata] mu;

vector<lower=0>[Ndata] beta_a;
    vector<lower=0>[Ndata] beta_b;

a ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    ph ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); // half-cauchy
    //sx ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); // half-cauchy
    sx ~ gamma(2.0, 4.0); 
    xtrue ~ normal(0, 3);
    x ~ normal(xtrue, sx);

for (n in 1:Ndata) {
      mu[n] <- inv_logit(a + b*xtrue[n]);
    }

beta_a <- mu * ph;
  beta_b <- (1-mu) * ph;
  y ~ beta(beta_a, beta_b);
}
"

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] beta regression on data with measurement error
parts:
What performed poorly? Were some parameters not mixing or was
it just slow?

I'm curious as to what priors Andrew or Ben would recommend.
I'd think providing a hierarhcical prior for xtrue would make sense,
but I'm not sure.

I'm thinking some kind of non-centered parameterization would
really help because of the multiplicative problem with b and xtrue
both being parameters:

sigma_xerr ~ ...;
xerr ~ normal(0, sx);
...
mu[n] <- inv_logit(a + b * (x[n] + xerr[n]));

The sx is still the measurement error scale.

- Bob

parts:
I’m not sure but it’s possible this model could have problems when the beta distribution parameters are near 0. I don’t know the context, but maybe you should ask yourself what kind of model you want for y. Do you really need the full range of beta distributions, including those U-shaped distributions with peaks at 0 and 1? Maybe simplest to just model y as normal on the logit scale.
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] beta regression on data with measurement error
parts:
The U-shaped issue isn’t as clear as it might sound. As we’ve discussed on the blackboard, you can write any (0,1) distribution as a (-inf,+inf) dist on the logit scale. Uniform on 0,1 correspoinds to a unit logistic (approx N(0,1.6), I believe) on logit scale. If you take N(0,sigma) on logit scale, then if sigma<1.6 (I think it is), you’ll get a unimodal distribution on the (0,1) scale, and if sigma>1.6, you get a bimodal or U-shaped distribution on the (0,1) scale. So, from that perspective, there’s nothing magic about the U-shape.

But the larger point remains valid, which is that existing functional forms (e.g., beta distribution) are often much more general than the models we have in mind. Hence the role of weakly informative priors. Without such priors, you’re really letting your modeling choices be driven by convention, in the sense of working with unbounded distirbutions that happen to have existing names.

A
